title: How a Viral Escalator Video Sparked Norway's World Cup Rallying Cry
summary:
It started with a video. Jeremy Siegel, a reporter for GBH in Boston, was at South Station when he heard a chorus of deep voices chanting "Row! Row! Row!" As the voices got closer, he saw a group of Norwegian soccer fans, wearing Viking helmets, sitting side by side on an escalator, rocking back and forth and pulling imaginary oars. He filmed it, tweeted it, and it went viral. The "Viking Row" was born.

Norway had qualified for the World Cup for the first time in 28 years, and thousands of fans descended on Boston. Alongside Scotland's famous "Tartan Army," they filled the city with energy. Bar owners noted that between the Scots and Norwegians, they ran out of beer. The Viking Row quickly became the nation's rallying cry. Fans did it in the stands during Norway's opening match, a 4-1 victory over Iraq.

The trend even reached Norway's parliament. Speaker Masud Gharahkhani led a special session where lawmakers grabbed imaginary oars and chanted. "We are doing it for peace. We are doing it for love and to show our support for the football team," he said. Parliamentary leader Tonje Brenna called it a homage to the national team.

For a country of just 5.6 million, this World Cup run is huge. "Norway is gripped by the tournament," said fan Veslemoy Aga. "We're dreaming of the World Cup." The Viking Row, inspired by ancient warriors, has become a symbol of unity and joy.
why_it_matters: This story shows how a simple, fun moment can unite a whole country and even reach political leaders, reminding us that shared joy can cross from sports into everyday life and national identity.

background_read: The FIFA World Cup is held every four years and is the most-watched sports event on the planet. Norway, a Scandinavian nation of 5.6 million people, had not qualified for the tournament since 1998, breaking a 28-year drought. The event will be co-hosted by the United States, Canada, and Mexico in 2026, which explains why thousands of Norwegian fans traveled to Boston (a major U.S. city and a host venue) for the early rounds. The 'Viking' nickname comes from Norse seafarers who explored and traded across Europe from the 8th to 11th centuries; today it also symbolizes a fierce, adventurous spirit. Scotland's 'Tartan Army' is the name for that country's devoted soccer supporters, known for wearing traditional plaid patterns. Jeremy Siegel—a journalist with GBH News, Boston's public radio station—was at South Station, a busy transit hub, when he recorded the chant that became an internet sensation.

perspectives.description: The Viking Row creates a strong sense of belonging and excitement, turning fans into active participants rather than just spectators.
Skeptics might say such simple chants distract from the serious money and politics in modern sports, reducing deeper issues to a fleeting viral trend.
Social media researchers note that viral cultural moments like this can boost national morale and tourism, but their impact often fades quickly once the event is over.
Whether this spontaneous chant becomes an enduring part of Norwegian soccer culture or remains a one-tournament gimmick depends on future teams and fans keeping the tradition alive.
